title: Reading charts critically
examples: How do I know if a graph is trying to trick me?
What should I look for when I see a chart in a report?
Can you give me an example of a bad graph?

explain.say: First we need to understand the axes on any chart.
The x-axis usually shows the categories or time passing.
The y-axis shows the actual measured quantity or amount.
Be careful when the y-axis starts at a number higher than zero.
A truncated scale exaggerates the difference between the data points.
A misleading visual uses a 3D effect to distort the actual data proportions.

faq.q: If the y-axis doesn't start at zero, how do I correct the reading?
faq.a: You must mentally redraw the axis to start at zero to see the true proportion. You can also calculate the true ratio yourself.
asks: How do I fix a graph that starts high?
What if the baseline is cut off?

faq.q: What is the best way to spot a misleading visual?
faq.a: Always check the y-axis labels and ensure the graph is presented in a simple 2D format. If it looks too dramatic, be suspicious.
asks: How do I check for distortion?

faq.q: Do I need to check the units on the axes?
faq.a: Yes, always verify the units like percentage or currency are consistent across all data points. Inconsistent units are a common trap.

faq.q: Can a graph be misleading without any obvious tricks?
faq.a: Yes, simply choosing the wrong scale or omitting necessary context can mislead. The context is just as important as the numbers shown.
asks: Are there subtle ways to mislead?

faq.q: What is the difference between a scale and a range?
faq.a: The scale is the interval markings on the axis, while the range is the actual minimum and maximum values displayed. They must match logically.
asks: What is the range of the data?

facts: The x-axis typically represents independent variables or time.
A truncated y-axis exaggerates small changes by cutting off the zero point.
Three-dimensional charts can distort the perceived size and magnitude of data.
Always check the units of measurement listed on both axes.

quiz.say: A chart shows sales increasing from 90 to 110 on the y-axis, but the axis starts at 80. What is the most accurate interpretation?

options.show: The increase is 20 units, regardless of the starting point.
options.say: The increase is 20 units, regardless of the starting point.

options.show: The increase is 20 points on the scale.
options.say: The increase is 20 points on the scale.

options.show: The increase is proportional to the visual height.
options.say: The increase is proportional to the visual height.

quiz.why: The difference between 110 and 90 is 20, which is the true change.

wrong.1: This mistakes the scale reading for the actual value change.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the difference between the start and end points.
wrong.3: Visual height is distorted by the truncated scale, so it is unreliable.

quiz.say: When analyzing a graph, what is the first thing you should check regarding the y-axis?
quiz.show: Correct: If it starts at zero

options.show: It should ideally start at zero to represent the full context.
options.say: It should ideally start at zero to represent the full context.

quiz.why: Starting at zero prevents artificial exaggeration of the data spread.

wrong.0: A linear scale is good, but a non-zero start point can still be misleading.
wrong.1: Being 2D only prevents one type of distortion; the scale itself can still be cut.
wrong.3: Units are important, but the zero baseline is the primary check for distortion.

quiz.say: If a bar chart uses a 3D effect, what is the immediate risk to the viewer?

options.show: The depth and perspective can make bars look taller or shorter than they are.
options.say: The depth and perspective can make bars look taller or shorter than they are.

quiz.why: The visual trickery of 3D often overrides the actual numerical data.

wrong.0: The 3D effect is a visual distortion, not an indication of a repeating cycle.
wrong.2: The x-axis labels are usually unaffected by the 3D rendering.
wrong.3: While scale reading is always key, the 3D effect specifically targets the bar comparison.
